observation: The prior finding that 'no DB row is newer than 2025-10-01' is FALSE for ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA. The database is live and being written to continuously. The newest business-table timestamp found is sso_services.ss_modified_on = 2026-08-03 15:29:18, i.e. minutes before the query ran. The newest timestamp anywhere is ArconPamApiLog.LoggedOnDate = 2026-08-03 14:23:35, rising during the session.
evidence: Query: SELECT 'sso_services.ss_modified_on', MAX(ss_modified_on), COUNT(*) FROM sso_services UNION ALL (18 further table/column pairs). Result, sorted descending: sso_services.ss_modified_on 2026-08-03 15:29:18 (20651 rows); sso_user_details.sud_created_on 2026-08-03 15:25:38; sso_users.created_on 2026-08-03 15:25:38; sso_users.modified_on 2026-08-03 15:13:40; sso_lobs_services.lsg_created_on 2026-08-03 14:27:27; sso_services.ss_created_on 2026-08-03 14:27:23. Corroborated by row counts rising between two counts in the same session: sso_services 20650 -> 20651, sso_user_td 99565 -> 99611, ssR_Users_Services 313086 -> 313197.
impact: Removes the blocker that made DB validation look pointless. The earlier conclusion was almost certainly drawn from a different database on the same instance, or from the empty ADbridging tables. Persistence assertions CAN be written against this database.
recommendation: Retract the 2025-10-01 statement wherever it is recorded and replace it with the measured value above. Always name the database when quoting a freshness figure - this instance hosts 31.

observation: The QA API's writes DO land in ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA. The 2026-07-29_181439 run created 7 business rows and modified 5, all traceable to the run.
evidence: Query: SELECT 'sso_services', COUNT(*) FROM sso_services WHERE ss_created_on BETWEEN '2026-07-29 18:14:39' AND '2026-07-29 21:35:00' UNION ALL (9 further tables). Results: sso_services 1, sso_users 1, sso_user_details 1, sso_lobs_users 1, sso_lobs_services 1, sso_services_param 1, sso_ApiUsers 1, sso_lobs 0, sso_Sgroup 0, sso_Ugroup 0. Modified in the same window: sso_services 3, sso_users 2. The created rows carry created_by='SYSTEM_API': sso_users ssu_id=1457 created_on 2026-07-29 19:12:03; sso_services ss_service_id=25342 ss_created_on 2026-07-29 19:12:38; sso_ApiUsers RowId=365 Username='AUTO40PC47' CreatedOn 2026-07-29 19:54:46.
impact: Three independent confirmations (audit log, business-table timestamps, plaintext SYSTEM_API stamp) that the API under test writes to this database. DB validation is therefore not merely possible but directly useful.
recommendation: Adopt DB validation for the 13 drivable create endpoints first, since exactly those are the ones whose writes are visible here.

observation: Column-level encryption is application-side and DETERMINISTIC: the same plaintext always produces the same ciphertext, with no per-row IV or salt, under a key shared across all columns and tables. This is functionally equivalent to AES-ECB.
evidence: Query: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT ss_port), COUNT(DISTINCT ss_server_ip), COUNT(DISTINCT ss_username) FROM sso_services -> 20651 rows but only 59 distinct ss_port ciphertexts; a single ciphertext '/QJnyC6c+u1e5VeF0EyvPA==' covers 18848 rows (91%). Query: the ciphertext '4QVsqJbF6MWeAvmlLMC+Kg==' appears in sso_lobs.sls_address2 (67 rows), sso_lobs.sls_report_header (123 rows) and sso_services.ss_instance (18865 rows) - three different columns across two different tables. The run-created sso_users row had ssu_username and ssu_displayname holding the identical ciphertext 'OhjN7MeS4xe7sCksQFhyTMUAKRTy1ZbFzZu+2KUHDAk='. Query: SELECT name, algorithm_desc FROM sys.symmetric_keys -> 0 rows; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sys.certificates -> 0. No TDE or Always Encrypted.
impact: Two consequences pulling in opposite directions. SECURITY: deterministic encryption leaks plaintext distribution - 91% of services sharing one port ciphertext tells an attacker with read access that they all use the default port, without needing the key. Frequency analysis recovers common values. TESTING: determinism is what makes ciphertext-equality lookups work, so it is also the reason DB validation is feasible at all.
recommendation: Raise the deterministic-encryption weakness as a product security defect: randomised IV per row, or SQL Server Always Encrypted with randomised encryption. Note that fixing it will BREAK ciphertext-equality validation, so the framework should prefer the audit-log lever (DB-005), which survives the fix.

observation: Encryption is NOT widespread - it is applied per column, and two of the seven surveyed business objects have no encryption at all. Encrypted: sso_lobs (5 of 7 text columns, including sls_name), sso_users (4, including ssu_username and ssu_displayname), sso_services (12, including ss_username, ss_server_ip, ss_server_host, ss_port), sso_user_details (2). Fully plaintext: sso_Sgroup, sso_Ugroup, sso_ApiUsers, sso_arcos_log.
evidence: Method: sample up to 4 non-null values per text column, classify by shape (base64 charset, length a multiple of 4, decodes to whole 16-byte AES blocks, printable-byte fraction below 0.75). Script: tools/obj007_encryption_survey.ps1. Verdicts: sso_lobs.sls_name ENCRYPTED '6riBmF0+uM8LEZjpHV4a2Q==' (16B, 1 block, frac 0.19); sso_lobs.sls_created_by PLAINTEXT; sso_Sgroup.srv_group_name PLAINTEXT (non-base64 chars); sso_Ugroup.usr_group_name PLAINTEXT; sso_users.ssu_username ENCRYPTED '+0PSggY5XiWZuQ1lBoTdWQ==' (16B, frac 0.38); sso_services.ss_username ENCRYPTED (16B, frac 0.25); sso_ApiUsers.Username PLAINTEXT 'AUTO40PC47'. Classification is INFERENCE - SQL Server reports all of these as plain varchar.
impact: The blanket assumption that 'names are encrypted so DB validation cannot work' is wrong. Service groups and user groups can be validated by direct plaintext name match today, with no key and no workaround.
recommendation: Pilot DB validation on sso_Sgroup and sso_Ugroup, where a plaintext name match is available, before tackling the encrypted objects.

observation: sso_arcos_log is a full change-audit table whose object references are PLAINTEXT, and it records API-originated writes distinguishably. This solves the encryption problem for validation: a created object can be matched by its real name even though the business table stores that name encrypted.
evidence: Structure: sal_id (bigint PK identity), sal_timestamp, sal_object_referance, sal_old_value, sal_new_value, aoo_object_operation, aot_description, sal_ipaddress, sal_Api_user_id, sal_user_id. Query for the run window filtered to the runner IP: SELECT sal_id, sal_timestamp, aoo_object_operation, aot_description, sal_object_referance, sal_Api_user_id FROM sso_arcos_log WHERE sal_timestamp BETWEEN '2026-07-29 18:14:39' AND '2026-07-29 21:35:00' AND sal_ipaddress='10.10.1.242' -> 5 rows: 2313798 19:12:06 Created 'User Transactions' 'AUTO40PC47' api=2; 2313799 19:12:42 Created 'Service Transactions' '10.11.0.48@SVC40PC47:Windows RDP' api=2; 2313801 19:27:20 Deleted 'Service Transactions' '10.10.0.38@arcostest12:SSHLINUX' api=2; 2313852 19:44:00 Created 'User Transactions' 'AUTO40PC47' api=2; 2313853 19:49:46 Created 'User Transactions' 'AUTO40PC47' api=2. Plaintext confirmed across 14 operation/object-type groupings. 23264 rows carry a non-null sal_Api_user_id out of 2267563.
impact: This is the primary validation channel. It covers create, update (via sal_old_value/sal_new_value) and delete, is immune to column encryption, and sal_Api_user_id separates API writes from UI writes so a test cannot be fooled by concurrent manual activity.
recommendation: Build DBUtils validation around sso_arcos_log as the primary assertion source, with the business table as the durability confirmation. Capture aot_description values per object type first - only 'User Transactions' and 'Service Transactions' were observed during the run.

observation: sso_arcos_log OVER-REPORTS record creation. It logs the attempt, not the durable insert. Six audit rows claim 'Created / User Transactions / AUTO40PC47' but only one sso_users row and one sso_ApiUsers row exist for that name.
evidence: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sso_arcos_log WHERE sal_object_referance='AUTO40PC47' AND aoo_object_operation='Created' AND aot_description='User Transactions' -> 6. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sso_users WHERE ssu_username='OhjN7MeS4xe7sCksQFhyTMUAKRTy1ZbFzZu+2KUHDAk=' -> 1. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sso_ApiUsers WHERE Username='AUTO40PC47' -> 1. Within the run window alone, 3 of those 6 audit 'Created' rows appeared (19:12:06, 19:44:00, 19:49:46) while sso_users gained exactly 1 row.
impact: An assertion built only on the audit log would pass a repeated create that actually inserted nothing. This is the DB-side mirror of the known API trap where Success:true carries Message:'Already Exists'. Confirms that neither channel is sufficient alone.
recommendation: Every create assertion must be two-part: audit log proves the API attempted and logged the operation; a business-table COUNT proves the row is durably there. Assert on both, and report them separately so a divergence is visible rather than averaged away.

observation: The API stamps a plaintext actor 'SYSTEM_API' into created_by / *_created_by, giving a decryption-free way to isolate API-created rows.
evidence: SELECT created_by, COUNT(*) FROM sso_users GROUP BY created_by -> 'SYSTEM_API' 11 rows, among 80 distinct actors (largest ARCOSADMIN 223). SELECT ss_created_by, COUNT(*) FROM sso_services GROUP BY ss_created_by -> 'SYSTEM_API' 395 rows among 65 distinct actors (largest ARCOSADMIN 15611). Both run-created rows carried it: sso_users ssu_id=1457 created_by='SYSTEM_API'; sso_services ss_service_id=25342 ss_created_by='SYSTEM_API'.
impact: Provides a cheap, encryption-independent filter for 'rows this API created', which combined with a timestamp window isolates a single test run's writes.
recommendation: Use created_by='SYSTEM_API' AND created_on >= @testStartUtc as the standard scoping predicate in DBUtils. Note it identifies the API as actor, not the individual test, so it needs the timestamp window to be run-specific.

observation: sso_ApiUsers stores API-user credentials in CLEARTEXT - Password, UsersSecret and UsersKey are all plaintext, in the same table as the username, while the far less sensitive sso_users.ssu_username is encrypted.
evidence: SELECT TOP 3 * FROM sso_ApiUsers WHERE CreatedOn BETWEEN '2026-07-29 18:14:39' AND '2026-07-29 21:35:00' -> RowId 365, Username 'AUTO40PC47', Password '<REDACTED>', UsersSecret '<REDACTED>', UsersKey '<REDACTED>', Active 1, Is_Locked False. Encryption survey of the table returned no ENCRYPTED verdict on any column.
impact: Any principal with SELECT on this one table obtains working API credentials plus the shared secret and key for every API user. The encryption applied elsewhere in the schema is undermined by this table. 34 API users are exposed.
recommendation: Raise as a product security defect. Passwords must be salted-hashed, not stored; UsersSecret and UsersKey must be encrypted at rest or held outside the database. Independently, restrict SELECT on sso_ApiUsers - the least-privilege validation account must NOT be granted it.

observation: Private key material is stored unencrypted in the application database, in the same database as the data it protects.
evidence: Table tbl_KeyEncryptionDecryption, columns ked_ID (bigint), ked_PublicKey (nvarchar(max)), ked_PrivateKey (nvarchar(max)), ked_Created_On, ked_Modified_On. SELECT ked_ID, LEN(ked_PublicKey), LEN(ked_PrivateKey), ked_Created_On FROM tbl_KeyEncryptionDecryption -> 1 row: ked_ID 351, public key length 460, private key length 1702, created 2026-08-02 13:00:14. Key material itself was deliberately NOT read. sys.symmetric_keys is empty and sys.certificates returns 0, so no native SQL Server key protection is in play.
impact: Read access to the database yields the private key, defeating the encryption in DB-003. The identity value of 351 on a single surviving row suggests the keypair is rotated and old rows deleted, which is good practice undermined by storing the material in cleartext.
recommendation: Move key material to a secret store or HSM (sso_hsm_config exists, suggesting HSM support is already available), or at minimum protect it with a SQL Server certificate. Exclude this table from any test account's grants.

observation: A background provisioning job is permanently broken, emitting a constant ~240 errors per hour indefinitely. It is unrelated to the test run and predates it. Two methods fail in lockstep, 770 occurrences each within the run window alone.
evidence: SELECT CONVERT(char(13), LoggedOnDate, 120), COUNT(*) FROM ArconPamApiLog WHERE LogId BETWEEN 38300000 AND 38700000 AND ApplicationName='ARCONPAMAPI' AND Method='CallBack' GROUP BY CONVERT(char(13), LoggedOnDate, 120) -> a flat 240 per hour across every complete hour from 2026-07-29 17:00 through 2026-07-30 03:00, spanning the run window unchanged (17h 240, 18h 240, 19h 240, 20h 240, 21h 240, 22h 240, 23h 240, 00h 240 ...). Failing pair: ARCONPAMAPI.Controllers.TargetDeviceOnboardingController.CallBack (message APA:DOC0010) and DataAccessLayer.Common.DatabaseCRUD.UpdateTargetUserCreationStatus (APA:DL0046), both with 'System.IndexOutOfRangeException: There is no row at position 0.' Source IP 10.10.0.120, distinct from the test runner's 10.10.1.242. Also visible in the live tail: ARCOSProvisioningReconService logging 'Incomplete Request Processing For delete user' and a RuntimeBinderException 'Cannot convert null to int'.
impact: Roughly 5,760 error rows per day, about 2.1M per year, from one broken loop. It inflated the run-window error count from 194 genuinely test-attributable rows to 1,736, and would mislead anyone attributing API errors to a test. It also means the target-device onboarding callback path is non-functional in QA.
recommendation: Raise as a product defect against the TargetDeviceOnboarding callback and UpdateTargetUserCreationStatus - it is a null/empty result set being indexed at position 0 without a guard. Separately, any DB-based error analysis must filter by source IP or ApplicationName before attributing errors to a test.

observation: The devops login used for validation is sysadmin and dbcreator, mapping to dbo in the target database, with 34 server-level and 82 database-level permissions over 31 databases.
evidence: SELECT r.name FROM sys.server_role_members m JOIN sys.server_principals r ON r.principal_id=m.role_principal_id JOIN sys.server_principals p ON p.principal_id=m.member_principal_id WHERE p.name='devops' -> 'sysadmin'. SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'), IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('dbcreator'), USER_NAME(), (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fn_my_permissions(NULL,'SERVER')) -> 1, 1, 'dbo', 34. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fn_my_permissions(NULL,'DATABASE') -> 82. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sys.databases -> 31. Server-scope permissions include ALTER ANY DATABASE, ALTER ANY LOGIN, ALTER ANY CREDENTIAL, ALTER ANY LINKED SERVER, ADMINISTER BULK OPERATIONS, ALTER SERVER STATE.
impact: An automated suite running as this login could drop or alter any of 31 databases, several non-QA, through a typo or a bad generated statement. The credential is committed in plaintext in Environments/QA_MsSQL.properties, so it is also in version control and on every CI agent.
recommendation: Provision a dedicated least-privilege login for validation and change QA_MsSQL.properties to use it. Required grants and the exact DDL are in docs/analysis/C-database-validation.md section 6: CONNECT plus SELECT on an explicit table whitelist, no server roles, no db_datareader, and explicit DENY on sso_ApiUsers and tbl_KeyEncryptionDecryption.

observation: ArconPamApiLog holds 41,910,875 rows with a single clustered primary key on LogId and no other index. LoggedOnDate, ApplicationName, Level and Method are all unindexed, so every date-range or application filter is a full scan of 41.9M rows.
evidence: SELECT i.name, i.type_desc, c.name, ic.key_ordinal FROM sys.indexes i JOIN sys.index_columns ic ... WHERE i.object_id=OBJECT_ID('ArconPamApiLog') -> exactly one row: PK_ArconPamApiLog, CLUSTERED, LogId, ordinal 1. Row count from sys.dm_db_partition_stats: 41910875. MIN(LoggedOnDate) 2020-08-13 17:07:03, MAX 2026-08-03 14:23:35, MAX(LogId) 41911659. Workaround used throughout this investigation: binary-search LogId to a date first (SELECT TOP 1 LogId, LoggedOnDate FROM ArconPamApiLog WHERE LogId >= N ORDER BY LogId, a clustered seek), then bound the real query by a LogId range.
impact: Naive log queries from a test or a support engineer will scan the whole table and can take minutes, on a database that is also serving the application. Six years of logs are retained with no partitioning or purge evident.
recommendation: Recommend a nonclustered index on (LoggedOnDate) and ideally (ApplicationName, LoggedOnDate) to the product team, plus a retention policy. In the framework, never filter this table by date alone - always bound by a LogId range first. Encode that rule in DBUtils.

observation: The run provoked 194 API-side error-log rows across 62 distinct methods from the test runner IP, including unhandled .NET exceptions that the HTTP 200 envelope concealed: InvalidCastException, OverflowException, NullReferenceException, SqlTypeException, FormatException and InvalidOperationException.
evidence: SELECT IpAddress, COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT Method) FROM ArconPamApiLog WHERE LogId BETWEEN 38300000 AND 38520000 AND ApplicationName='ARCONPAMAPI' AND LoggedOnDate BETWEEN '2026-07-29 18:14:00' AND '2026-07-29 21:35:00' GROUP BY IpAddress -> 10.10.0.120: 1540 rows / 2 methods (the DB-010 background loop); 10.10.1.242: 194 rows / 62 methods (the test runner); 'NOT AVAILABLE': 2 rows. Specific exceptions from the runner IP: GetUserDataDetailsV3 'System.InvalidCastException: Object cannot be cast...' x3; GetUserDataDetailsNew 'System.OverflowException: Value was either too lar...' x2; GetConfigById 'System.NullReferenceException: Object reference no...' x2; GetImgCapturedDet and GetUserSessionID 'System.Data.SqlTypes.SqlTypeException: SqlDateTime...'; GetImgCounterDet 'System.InvalidOperationException: The stored proce...'; SetDefaultTargetUser 'System.FormatException: Failed to convert paramete...'; IsComProSecureGatewayServerStart 'In IsComProSecureGatewayServerStart Exception----'.
impact: Confirms from the server side that HTTP-status assertions are worthless on this API - the server was throwing unhandled framework exceptions while returning 200. Also demonstrates that the DB error log surfaces defects invisible to a black-box API test.
recommendation: Treat ArconPamApiLog as a first-class assertion source: after a functional test, assert that the run produced no new ERROR rows for the runner IP. That single check would have flagged all 62 methods. Raise the specific unhandled exceptions as product defects.

observation: Application error codes recorded in the database follow 902-* and 903-* families that the framework does not recognise. ApiHelper's KNOWN_ERROR_CODES = {201, 202, 203} is far smaller than the real code space.
evidence: From the run-window error rows at IP 10.10.1.242 (query as in DB-013, grouped by Method and Message): '903- SDC-SFS' (GetServiceDetailsFromSession, 9), '903- SDC-USL' (ModifyData / SetUserSessionLogout / GetRecentServices), '902-UDC-ULN' (GetUserListByNameNew / GetAllUserDetails), '902-SDC-ATU' (GetUserPasswordLessLogin), '902-AC-GASU', '902-AC-GAPU', '902-AC-GAUD', '902SPB-GSP', '902SPC-GSP', '902SPD-GSP' (GetServicePassword, three distinct codes), '902-RAC-GIC', '902-RAC-ICD', '902-NBL-SPRN', '902-LSC-GLSTL-', '902-FS-DFS', '902-STC-GST-', '902-AB-SAC-', '902-SPC-GTDOS-', '903-HUM-WDTAKV', '903-GUL', '903-SDC-GCBI', '903-SDC-GSDSIN', '903- GAC', '903- GCD', '903- VSR-GSD', 'APA:DL0046', 'APA:DL0048', 'APA:DL0063', 'APA:DL0045', 'APA:DOC0010', 'APA:DOC0012', 'APA:Decrypt0001', 'API:AL0001'. Also observed: 'APA:Decrypt0001 - PlainText -auto40pc47@test.local' at 19:54:46, matching the sso_ApiUsers row created at that second.
impact: Extends the brief's finding that KNOWN_ERROR_CODES is incomplete, and shows the codes are structured (family-controller-method) rather than plain integers, so a numeric-only set can never match them. A single endpoint can emit several distinct codes.
recommendation: Harvest the full code catalogue from ArconPamApiLog rather than guessing: SELECT DISTINCT Message FROM ArconPamApiLog WHERE ApplicationName='ARCONPAMAPI' AND Level='ERROR' bounded by a LogId range. Replace the hardcoded set with data loaded from that catalogue.

observation: The database declares only 5 foreign keys in total across 552 tables. Referential integrity is enforced only in application code, and measurable orphan rows exist as a result.
evidence: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sys.foreign_keys -> 5. Among sso*/ssR* tables only 4 are declared: sso_ApiUsers.CreatedByUserId -> sso_users.ssu_id, sso_ApiUsers.UpdatedByUserId -> sso_users.ssu_id, sso_arcos_validation_operation.PT_ID -> sso_arcos_parametertype.ID, sso_services_asv.asv_ark_id -> sso_services_ark.ark_id. Measured orphans: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ssR_Users_Services rs LEFT JOIN sso_services s ON s.ss_service_id=rs.sus_service_id WHERE s.ss_service_id IS NULL -> 16560 of 313197 (5.3%); SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sso_lobs_users lu LEFT JOIN sso_users u ON u.ssu_id=lu.lug_ssu_id WHERE u.ssu_id IS NULL -> 9 of 1147; the same join against sso_lobs -> 1 orphan LOB; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sso_users u LEFT JOIN sso_user_details d ON d.sud_user_id=u.ssu_id WHERE d.sud_user_id IS NULL -> 17 of 1439.
impact: 16,560 user-to-service mappings point at services that no longer exist - deletion does not cascade and leaves dangling authorisation rows. In a privileged-access product, orphaned access mappings are a security-relevant data-integrity defect, not merely untidy data. It also means integrity validation is both possible and immediately productive.
recommendation: Raise the 16,560 orphans as a product defect. Add the four queries above to the framework as standing integrity assertions - they need no encryption handling and would regress-guard every delete path.

observation: Link tables carry denormalized copies of parent values that have measurably drifted from the authoritative rows.
evidence: sso_lobs_users duplicates lug_ssu_username and lug_sls_name; sso_lobs_services duplicates nine parent columns (lsgr_sls_name, lsgr_ss_server_ip, lsgr_ss_server_host, lsgr_ss_username, lsgr_ss_domain_name, lsgr_ss_instance, lsgr_ss_created_by, lsgr_ss_created_on, lsgr_tbv_description). Query: SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(CASE WHEN lu.lug_sls_name=l.sls_name THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), SUM(CASE WHEN lu.lug_sls_name<>l.sls_name THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), SUM(CASE WHEN l.sls_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM sso_lobs_users lu LEFT JOIN sso_lobs l ON l.sls_id=lu.lug_sls_id -> total 1147, matching 472, DRIFTED 5, orphan LOB 1. The remaining 669 have a NULL on one side.
impact: Gives consistency validation a concrete, encryption-independent target: the copy must equal the authoritative value. Comparing ciphertext to ciphertext works precisely because encryption is deterministic (DB-003). 5 rows are already wrong, so the check finds real defects on day one.
recommendation: Implement the drift query as a consistency assertion. Report the 5 existing drifted rows to the product team as a data-integrity defect, and re-baseline before enabling the assertion in CI so pre-existing drift does not fail every run.

observation: The ADbridging and data-warehouse table families are entirely empty, confirming and widening the prior tblLOBDetail finding.
evidence: Row counts from sys.dm_db_partition_stats (index_id in (0,1)) are 0 for: tblLOBDetail, tblADUserDetails, tblassigneduser, tblRuleGroupAssocRoles, tblRuleRoleOnAdAssocRoles, sso_AD_users, sso_AD_users_dump, sso_AD_groups, sso_AD_groups_dump, sso_AD_services, sso_AD_services_dump, sso_ob_AD_users, sso_ob_AD_users_dump, sso_ob_AD_groups, sso_ob_AD_groups_dump, sso_ob_AD_services, sso_ob_AD_services_dump, sso_ob_AdmUser, sso_ob_LocalUsers, sso_ob_UserLobs, sso_ob_User_rule, sso_ob_Globalconfig, DWH_LOBSERVICEMAPPING, DWH_LOBUSERMAPPING, dwh_LobSGroupMapping, dwh_LobUserGroupMapping, Dwh_ServiceMaster, Dwh_ServiceSgroupMapping, Dwh_TimeBasedServicesMapping, Dwh_UgroupSgroupMapping, dwh_UserGroupMapping, dwh_UserMaster, Dwh_UserServiceMapping, Dwh_UserSgroupMapping, Dwh_AuditDetails. Also empty: the four access-control profile tables and sso_user_service_permissions. Non-empty counterparts exist: tblUsers has 1 row, tblADUserStatusDetail 6, tblRuleUserAssocRoles 2.
impact: No AD-bridging or data-warehouse functionality can be validated against this database - there is no data. Any endpoint whose reads or writes target these tables will appear to succeed while asserting nothing. The DWH emptiness is consistent with the GenericScheduler ETL account being locked.
recommendation: Mark AD-bridging and DWH endpoints as out of scope for DB validation and record why. If they must be covered, request seeded AD-bridge data, and note that the locked GenericScheduler account likely has to be unlocked for the DWH tables to populate.

observation: Deletion is validated only through the audit log, because the product performs hard deletes with no tombstone on the main business tables. Purge tables exist but are separate and partially populated.
evidence: The run's delete is present in the audit log: sal_id 2313801, 2026-07-29 19:27:20, aoo_object_operation 'Deleted', aot_description 'Service Transactions', sal_object_referance '10.10.0.38@arcostest12:SSHLINUX', sal_Api_user_id 2, IP 10.10.1.242. It correlates with ArconPamApiLog rows at 19:26:56 from the same IP: DelServiceDataDetails message '903' and 'System.Exception: Selected Service May Not Availab...', and SetDeleteService message '902-SCC-SDE'. No is_deleted or status column was found on sso_services during the encryption survey. Separate purge tables exist with rows: sso_services_purge 4176, ssR_Users_Services_purge 1952, sso_lobs_services_purge 111, sso_services_param_purge 101, sso_password_envolop_reprint_log_purge 2016; others are empty (sso_services_interface_purge, sso_windowsconnection_services_purge, sso_user_restricted_processes_profile_purge).
impact: Delete validation must assert absence, which is weaker than asserting presence: a row absent because the delete worked is indistinguishable from a row that never existed. The audit log entry plus a before/after count is the only sound formulation. Note the API logged an exception on the same delete, so the operation was audited as 'Deleted' while the server threw.
recommendation: Formulate delete assertions as three-part: capture the PK before deleting, assert the audit log has a 'Deleted' row for that plaintext reference after, and assert the business row no longer matches that PK. Never assert absence alone.

observation: The L6 record-exists layer cannot settle whether a create happened. 97 of its 107 checks searched for the literal unresolved string ${NEW_ID} and could never have passed, so the '105 of 107 failed' figure is largely a harness artifact, not a product measurement. For 101 of 107 hops the run cannot separate 'never created' from 'created but not readable back'. A read-only SELECT on ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA is the only thing that can distinguish the two.
evidence: Prior measured tally (docs/history/archive/document-agent-brief.md section 3): L6 ran on 107 hops, PASS 2, FAIL 105; all 196 L5 chain-key failures carry the identical detail 'resolved []; MISSING [NEW_ID]'. Harness analysis established that 97 of the 107 L6 checks searched for the literal ${NEW_ID}, leaving 101 of 107 indeterminate. Database side, measured for the same window: 7 business rows created (sso_services, sso_users, sso_user_details, sso_lobs_users, sso_lobs_services, sso_services_param, sso_ApiUsers - 1 each) and 5 modified (sso_services 3, sso_users 2), plus 5 audit rows at the runner IP (2 creates, 1 delete). Queries as in DB-002 and DB-005.
impact: The existing check is structurally incapable of answering the question it was written to answer, and its failure count cannot be read as a defect count. Two of the writes it missed were nonetheless real and durable, which is the direct argument for a DB channel: only the database separates the three outcomes - never created, created but unreadable, created and readable.
recommendation: Replace L6 with a DB-backed existence check for the 13 drivable create endpoints. Report L6 as NOT-APPLICABLE, not FAIL, wherever no identifier was extracted and no DB channel exists, so harness artifacts stop being counted as product defects. Re-state the 105 figure wherever it is quoted.

observation: The database independently corroborates that most creates never happened. Across all 177 populated tables carrying a creation timestamp, only 110 rows appeared in the entire 3h20m run window, and only about 7 of those are business objects the API was asked to create. This is consistent with 117 of the 196 chaining failures being genuine create failures.
evidence: Swept every (table, created-column) pair where the table has rows and the column is a datetime named like created_on / CreatedOn / created_date, excluding *_purge tables - 177 pairs. Query pattern: SELECT '<tbl>.<col>', COUNT(*) FROM [<tbl>] WHERE [<col>] BETWEEN '2026-07-29 18:14:39' AND '2026-07-29 21:35:00', unioned across all 177. Total 110 rows. Breakdown: sso_arcos_log_details 63, sso_arcos_customcol_report 22, sso_arcos_report_download 4, sso_arcos_wft_details 3, sso_arcos_file_storage_log 2, sso_user_access_review 2, then 1 each in sso_lobs_services (two columns), sso_lobs_users, sso_user_details, sso_ApiUserAccessMapping, sso_server_type, sso_ApiUsers, sso_users_securitysettings, sso_services_param, sso_services, asm_ServerDetails, sso_file_server_detail, sso_users, sso_ats_preference_master. The largest contributors are logging and report side-effect tables, not business objects.
impact: Confirms the absence rather than contradicting it: against 217 create endpoints and 196 chaining failures, the database gained roughly 7 business rows. Had the run silently created hundreds of objects the API failed to report, this sweep would have shown it. It did not, so the API-side conclusion and the database agree.
recommendation: Use this sweep as the standard post-run reconciliation: one query, no decryption needed, and it proves in a single number whether a run's writes match its reported outcomes. Store the 110-row baseline so future runs are compared against it.

observation: The run window contains substantial write activity from other users and background jobs, so a bare before/after row count is not a safe assertion on this database.
evidence: Audit rows in the run window came from at least five distinct sources: 10.10.1.242 (the test runner, 5 rows), 10.10.6.88 (LAP1140, workflow and transaction changes), 10.10.0.203 (QATest), 10.10.1.123 (created 'Server Type Configuration' / 'Dynamic Test' at 18:37:11 - which explains the sso_server_type row in the DB-021 sweep), 10.10.8.215 (DSK056, modified Global Configuration at 19:18:15), plus 52 'Revoked' rows at 19:32:00-19:32:01 with a blank IP from an automatic revocation job. Operation mix in the window: Revoked 52, Created 6, Modified 5, Assigned 2, Deleted 2 - only 3 of which belong to the runner IP. Separately, DB-010 documents a background loop writing 240 error rows per hour throughout.
impact: Row-count-delta validation would attribute other people's writes to the test, and this QA environment is shared. Of the 6 'Created' audit rows in the window, only 2 were the test's.
recommendation: Never assert on a bare COUNT(*) delta. Always scope by an attribution predicate - created_by='SYSTEM_API', or sal_Api_user_id IS NOT NULL, or sal_ipaddress = the runner IP - combined with a timestamp window. DBUtils should make the unscoped count impossible to call.

observation: Environments/QA_MsSQL.properties now carries populated DB settings, and they point at the sysadmin login.
evidence: Grep of Environments/QA_MsSQL.properties lines 77-82: db_host_name=10.10.0.194, db_port=1433, databaseName=ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA, db_user=devops, db_password=<REDACTED>, db_type=mssql. Independently confirms the owner's answer on the QA target database. The credential is in plaintext in a version-controlled file.
impact: DBUtils can now connect, but as sysadmin. Combined with DB-011 this is the single highest-risk item in enabling DB validation: a generated or mistyped statement would execute with full destructive authority over 31 databases.
recommendation: Do not enable DB validation in CI until db_user points at the least-privilege account specified in docs/analysis/C-database-validation.md section 6. Add a startup guard in DBUtils that refuses to run if IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin') returns 1, and enforce read-only at the connection level.
